power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: The treatment prevalence of mental health problems among children and adolescents has risen significantly in recent decades.
It is unclear whether the increase in treatment prevalence is caused by changes in epidemiological prevalence.
Method: A systematic review and meta-analysis of repeated cross-sectional studies involving children and adolescents up to the age of 18 was conducted.
The review included studies from around the world that were carried out using identical study designs at least twice in the same region.
Results: 58 publications were included, with data collected between 1973 and 2023.
The overall odds ratio for changes in prevalence was 1.38 (95% confidence interval 1.26-1.52).
This corresponds to a risk ratio of 1.32.
The odds ratio for females was 1.47 (95% CI: 1.28-1.70), and the odds ratio for males was 1.25 (95% CI: 1.09-1.43).
The greatest increase in prevalence was observed in the pandemic decade of 2020.
Discussion: The overall result corresponds to a 3.7% increase in prevalence over the entire 50year period.
This can be interpreted as a slight increase.
Conclusion: The rise in psychiatric treatment for children and adolescents is not primarily due to an increase in epidemiological prevalence.
The mental health of children and adolescents has received considerable attention in recent years, both in the scientific community and in public debate.

The Lancet Psychiatry Commission on Youth Mental Health recently identified a global mental health crisis in children and adolescents, due to rising treatment rates and other deteriorating issues such increasing loneliness (McGorry et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The Lancet Psychiatry Commission on Youth Mental Health recently identified a global mental health crisis in children and adolescents, due to rising treatment rates and other deteriorating issues such increasing loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(McGorry et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The issue of media consumption in this context has been of great public concern (Haidt, 2024), suggesting that the youth mental health crisis started with the widespread utilization of smartphones in the 2010s which is now approaching universality.
text.formatted: The issue of media consumption in this context has been of great public concern <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Haidt, 2024)</ref>, suggesting that the youth mental health crisis started with the widespread utilization of smartphones in the 2010s which is now approaching universality.

text.text: Other factors considered relevant to the perceived crisis include climate breakdown, loneliness, body dissatisfaction, childhood maltreatment, extremist political attitudes, dysfunctional parenting, and the decline in freedom to engage in independent activities such as playing outside supervised areas.

Additionally, both in research and in health policy, the conviction has prevailed that the COVID-19 pandemic has had the most substantial negative psychosocial consequences for this age group with its impact extending for several years beyond the initial peaks of the crisis (Panchal et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Additionally, both in research and in health policy, the conviction has prevailed that the COVID-19 pandemic has had the most substantial negative psychosocial consequences for this age group with its impact extending for several years beyond the initial peaks of the crisis <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Panchal et al., 2023</ref>).

text.text: An associated trend was the significantly increasing rates of treatment for young people with mental disorders.
Even before the pandemic, there was a surge in young people seeking psychological treatment and being prescribed psychotropic drugs (Collishaw, 2015; Steinhausen, 2015).
text.formatted: Even before the pandemic, there was a surge in young people seeking psychological treatment and being prescribed psychotropic drugs <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Collishaw, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Steinhausen, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The increase in treatments for autism and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder has attracted particular attention.
In various countries, this development has even led to political reactions regarding research into the causes or the issue of overdiagnosis (Pearson, 2025).
text.formatted: In various countries, this development has even led to political reactions regarding research into the causes or the issue of overdiagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Pearson, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, it is unclear whether the increase in therapeutic treatments has anything to do with the 'true' prevalence (Richter et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, it is unclear whether the increase in therapeutic treatments has anything to do with the 'true' prevalence <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Richter et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Treatment prevalence studies have the disadvantage that the characteristics of the care system can be decisive (for example, access to treatment or treatment capacities) and, therefore, do not accurately reflect the underlying prevalence of mental health problems.
Before we describe further epidemiological aspects, we must clarify a terminological issue.
In the remainder of this article, we will use the term 'mental health problems' to describe the characteristic we are investigating.
We use this term for two reasons.

Firstly, the concept of 'mental illness' remains controversial among service users and, secondly, as explained in detail below, we include studies that have used symptoms or syndromes such as 'behavioural problems' or 'distress'.
Such characteristics also do not meet the criteria of the DSM or ICD classification systems, so that the term 'disorder' cannot be applied here.
'Mental health problems' can be seen as an umbrella concept that encompasses all variants (Richter & Dixon, 2023).
text.formatted: 'Mental health problems' can be seen as an umbrella concept that encompasses all variants <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Richter & Dixon, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The question of whether the prevalence of mental health problems have increased in children and adolescents has long been the subject of epidemiological research (Rutter & Smith, 1995).
text.formatted: The question of whether the prevalence of mental health problems have increased in children and adolescents has long been the subject of epidemiological research <ref type="bibr">(Rutter & Smith, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Given the well-established epidemiological observation that 50 per cent of all first manifestations of mental disorders have occurred by the age of 19 or 20 (McGrath et al., 2023), the question of increasing mental health problems is of interest to the entire field of mental health care, beyond children and adolescent care.
text.formatted: Given the well-established epidemiological observation that 50 per cent of all first manifestations of mental disorders have occurred by the age of 19 or 20 <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(McGrath et al., 2023)</ref>, the question of increasing mental health problems is of interest to the entire field of mental health care, beyond children and adolescent care.

text.text: Two earlier global reviews (without metaanalyses) from the mid-2010s concluded that the prevalence of mental health problems of children and adolescents had hardly changed at all over the previous decades, with only internalizing symptoms in young women showing such an increase (Bor et al., 2014; Collishaw, 2015).
text.formatted: Two earlier global reviews (without metaanalyses) from the mid-2010s concluded that the prevalence of mental health problems of children and adolescents had hardly changed at all over the previous decades, with only internalizing symptoms in young women showing such an increase <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bor et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Collishaw, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, in addition, numerous behaviours associated with substance use, abuse and dependence that are classified as risky have declined significantly in recent decades (Grucza et al., 2016; Twenge, 2023).
text.formatted: However, in addition, numerous behaviours associated with substance use, abuse and dependence that are classified as risky have declined significantly in recent decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Grucza et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Twenge, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Besides treatment prevalence, the predominant methodological approaches in this context include (1) longitudinal cohort studies and (2) repeated cross-sectional studies.
The longitudinal design not only reflects changes in prevalence over time but also reflects the ageing process of the study participants.
In view of the biological and social changes in adolescence, longitudinal study designs are therefore subject to considerable uncertainty.
From an epidemiological perspective, repeated cross-sectional studies are best suited to investigate prevalence changes that are solely attributable to the time factor (Richter et al., 2019).
text.formatted: From an epidemiological perspective, repeated cross-sectional studies are best suited to investigate prevalence changes that are solely attributable to the time factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Richter et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To the best of our knowledge, there has been no meta-analysis that is based exclusively on repeated cross-sectional studies on changes in the prevalence of mental health problems in children and underage adolescents.

Existing meta-analyses pool studies with different designs (Ludwig-Walz et al., 2022 , 2023) or use the year of data collection to compare point prevalence rates among different publications (Deng et al., 2023; Shorey et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Existing meta-analyses pool studies with different designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ludwig-Walz et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">, 2023)</ref> or use the year of data collection to compare point prevalence rates among different publications <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Deng et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Shorey et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, another meta-analysis used the timing of data collection during the COVID-19 pandemic to address temporal changes of point prevalence rates (Racine et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Similarly, another meta-analysis used the timing of data collection during the COVID-19 pandemic to address temporal changes of point prevalence rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Racine et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, these approaches are less effective from an epidemiological perspective, as it cannot be ensured that the pooled studies have the same research designs.
We are only aware of three meta-studies that address similar issues in some way, but each of these have methodological issues which we seek to improve upon.
One of the meta-studies analysed psychosomatic complaints surveyed in repeated cross-sectional studies between 1982 and 2013 (Potrebny et al., 2017).
text.formatted: One of the meta-studies analysed psychosomatic complaints surveyed in repeated cross-sectional studies between 1982 and 2013 <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Potrebny et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The meta-analysis yielded a pooled significant odds ratio of 1.04, which was interpreted by the authors as a minor increase.
However, these psychosomatic diagnoses are not part of the core mental health construct and cannot meaningfully be applied beyond its specific focus.
The two other meta-studies known to us used a similar analysis method to the study presented here to a certain extent worked with data from the Global Burden of Disease project.
The first of these studies focused on Europe exclusively and examined, among other things, changes in prevalence between 1990 and 2019 (Castelpietra et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The first of these studies focused on Europe exclusively and examined, among other things, changes in prevalence between 1990 and 2019 <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Castelpietra et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This study found, for example, increasing rates of anxiety disorders, but decreasing rates of depressive disorders and alcoholrelated disorders.
Unfortunately, no overall prevalence rates were reported.
The second study had a global focus (Yang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The second study had a global focus <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Yang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Based on the same age range up to 24 years, the global meta-regression analyses showed a significant increase in the global prevalence of mental disorders between 1990 and 2019, but these changes were primarily demographically driven.
The estimated age-standardized prevalence showed virtually no change.

However, in many cases, the Global Burden of Disease studies do not work with collected data but are based on metaregressions of numerous contextual factors, which are then used to estimate prevalence rates (Murray, 2022).
text.formatted: However, in many cases, the Global Burden of Disease studies do not work with collected data but are based on metaregressions of numerous contextual factors, which are then used to estimate prevalence rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Murray, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In this respect, there is much uncertainty regarding the reported changes in prevalence.
There is a clear need to gather prevalence rates from general population groups to inform professionals and warrant plans and priorities for policy makers.
Estimating changes in the extent of children and adolescents' mental health problems will further support the current need in health care provision and future improvement in service planning.
It will also inform an important topic in contemporary public debate.

Although previous studies have reported prevalence of mental health problems in children and adolescents, to our knowledge there has been no attempt to consolidate these prevalence rates globally using repeated cross-sectional studies.

The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to examine global prevalence rates over time in mental health problems amongst children and adolescents (4-18 years) in studies using repeated cross-sectional population surveys with specific reference to changes since the onset of COVID-19.
The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines have been followed.
The study is registered with Prospero (CRD42019121701).
We followed the study registration with minor changes related to subgroup analyses.
Ethical approval was not required for the study.
Inclusion criteria were applied to publications reporting repeated cross-sectional studies with at least two time points on any kind of mental problem in children and adolescents (4-18years).
When a study reported multiple survey waves, the first and last observation point were included.
We used a range of methods to define mental health problems.
We included formal diagnoses based on DSM as well as those based on validated self-report symptom and distress scales.
We included studies reporting in the following languages: English, French, German, and Dutch.
No time restrictions or geographical restrictions were applied.

Exclusion criteria comprised: longitudinal and cohort study designs which assessed the same population at both time points; treatment prevalence studies (including consumption of medication or prescriptions); studies in which the diagnosis was not core to the mental health construct, for example substance use/misuse, psychosomatic symptoms or personality traits; studies on suicides, suicidality or self-harm.
The search was performed on the following databases: Medline (Ovid), Psychinfo and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature.
The search was conducted across all databases in May 2023 and updated in March 2025.
The primary search process was conducted by AD and DR (see appendix for search strategy).
The filter limited to ages (birth-childhood, adolescents-18 years) was selected.
The study selection process was conducted by all authors who were paired to screen a selection of publications in batches.
Duplicates were identified and removed electronically and then manually.
Screening comprised reading titles and abstracts at stage 1, then full texts of selected studies at stage 2.
Disagreement on inclusion was resolved by consulting the lead author (DR).

When multiple studies reported different analyses of the same dataset over the same time period, the most representative study was selected (e.g., the study with the longest timeframe) and all the other studies were excluded.
To assess the risk of bias, a quality appraisal was carried out for all included studies.
As the current instruments were not suitable for our purposes of appraising repeated cross-sectional population studies specifically, we adapted an instrument by Munn et al (Munn et al., 2015).
text.formatted: As the current instruments were not suitable for our purposes of appraising repeated cross-sectional population studies specifically, we adapted an instrument by Munn et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Munn et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Higher scores were given to publications that had: national representativeness, clearly stated age range, random sampling, sample size greater than 500 per time point, description of subjects and settings, response rate of at least 80% or at least 50% with explicit justification, utilisation of a DSM or ICD related tool or validated instrument, identical procedures at both time points and a statistical analysis which was sufficiently described.
The same pairs of reviewers conducted quality appraisal independently then discussed within their pairs the final quality score.
The risk of bias assessment is provided in the appendix.
Data extraction was conducted by DR and 5% of papers were cross-checked by AD.

We included the following for data extraction; authors, publication year, country, world region, first data point year, second/last datapoint year, source of response (child, parent, teacher), mental health problem (depression, anxiety etc.), type of assessment (clinical diagnosis, symptoms, distress) and instrument used, number of cases per time point, youngest/oldest age, decade of first/last sample, sample size per time point, data collection during COVID-19 and quality appraisal score.
When studies reported percentages only and the sample size, we calculated and extracted the raw counts from these variables as required for effect size calculation by the statistical software.
The analytical strategy followed the procedure of a previous study on prevalence changes of mental disorders in adults (Richter et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The analytical strategy followed the procedure of a previous study on prevalence changes of mental disorders in adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Richter et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We utilised a methodology which is usually applied to intervention studies that compare intervention and control conditions with odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals (CI hereafter) as the effect size metric.

The first time point constituted a baseline or control assessment and was used as a control condition and the second or last time point was comparable to a post-intervention assessment to find out whether changes have occurred.
In other words, we considered 'time' as a form of intervention.
Current taxonomy research on mental disorders postulates a higher order of spectra (HiTOP) or even a general psychopathology beyond DSM/ICD classifications (Kotov et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Current taxonomy research on mental disorders postulates a higher order of spectra (HiTOP) or even a general psychopathology beyond DSM/ICD classifications <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Kotov et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For this reason, we pooled all effect sizes to identify a general trend regarding the prevalence of mental health problems independent of the underlying construct.
Most studies reported their results separately for each gender, but some reported results aggregated across genders.
Therefore, we conducted three main analyses: total (encompassing both genders), females, and males.
Due to this circumstance, primary observations in the gendered analyses do not add up to the total observations.

For sub-group analyses over time, we conducted an analysis of all studies and then compared pre-pandemic studies (both timepoints prior to 2020) with studies that had at least one timepoint in or after 2020.
We also conducted an analysis separately for each decade based on the year of the second timepoint (1990s, 2000s, 2010s, 2020s).
text.formatted: We also conducted an analysis separately for each decade based on the year of the second timepoint <ref type="bibr">(1990s, 2000s, 2010s, 2020s)</ref>.

text.text: The aim of this latter analysis was to determine whether certain decades showed a particular increase.
Finally, we performed a meta-regression with the aim of exploring moderators of between-study heterogeneity.
Peters' regression test was used to check for publication bias (Peters et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Peters' regression test was used to check for publication bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Peters et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: We used R (version 4.5.3) package 'meta' (version 8.2-1) (Schwarzer et al., 2015) and package 'metafor' (version 4.8-0) (Viechtbauer, 2010) with random effects models for the statistical analyses.
text.formatted: We used R (version 4.5.3) package 'meta' (version 8.2-1) <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Schwarzer et al., 2015)</ref> and package 'metafor' (version 4.8-0) <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Viechtbauer, 2010)</ref> with random effects models for the statistical analyses.

text.text: We also used the R package 'effectsize' (version 1.0.1) to convert odds ratio into risk ratio (Ben-Shachar et al., 2020).
text.formatted: We also used the R package 'effectsize' (version 1.0.1) to convert odds ratio into risk ratio <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ben-Shachar et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This is due to the general recommendation to report risk ratios instead of odds ratios, as they are easier to understand (Grant, 2014; van Rhee & Suurmond, 2015).
text.formatted: This is due to the general recommendation to report risk ratios instead of odds ratios, as they are easier to understand <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Grant, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">van Rhee & Suurmond, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Effect sizes such as the odds ratio or risk ratio are often not interpreted appropriately and tend to cause confusion due to their statistical and verbal characteristics (odds vs. risk) (Grant, 2014; Voas & Watt, 2025).
text.formatted: Effect sizes such as the odds ratio or risk ratio are often not interpreted appropriately and tend to cause confusion due to their statistical and verbal characteristics (odds vs. risk) <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Grant, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Voas & Watt, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A higher or lower risk between two groups is easier to understand than a higher or lower odds.
Our search identified 4829 publications from databases.
We assessed 213 publications in full text, and 58 studies were selected for inclusion (see Flow Chart, Appendix).
Of these 46 studies were conducted entirely prior to the COVID-19 pandemic and 12 had at least one timepoint during the COVID-19 period.
Altogether, 540,006 primary observations were included for the first time point and 520,672 primary observations for the second and last time points in the total analysis.
We identified several characteristics from the studies. 36 samples were from Europe, with a further 6 samples from Asia, 5 from Oceania, 3 from South America and 8 from North America.
Of the 58 studies 40 were based on instruments in which the child or adolescent self-reported on their condition.
The rest of the studies were based on reports by others (carers or teachers) or a combination of sources (carers, teachers and children/adolescents).
Carers and teachers were the main source in samples involving very young children. 31 studies reported data separately for females and 31 for males.
The overall time-range for baseline estimates was 50 years, ranging from 1973 to 2023.
The average duration between the first and the last year within each study that reported total data was 11.7 years (median: 10 years).
The baseline sample sizes were very heterogeneous and ranged from 279 to 242,734.

In terms of mental health problems, we found 36 studies covering general and behavioural problems, 15 covering depression, 9 covering general mental health issues, 4 covering eating disorders, 2 covering anxiety and 1 insomnia.
Risk of bias analyses indicated that the quality of the studies ranged from moderate to good. 37 of the 58 included studies scored 6 or more out of a possible 9 points.
The main analysis (Table 1) revealed a total odds ratio of 1.38 (95%-confidence interval: 1.26-1.52, I² = 99%, τ² = 0.13, p = 0.000), see also Forest Plot (Appendix).

text.text: The publications with the female data showed an odds ratio of 1.47 (95%-CI: 1.21-1.65), while the publications with the male data showed an odds ratio of 1.25 (95%-CI: 1.06-1.47).
We found a high heterogeneity in the pooled effect sizes of the total sample, the female sample, and the male sample (more than 90%).
The overall odds ratio of 1.38 corresponds to a risk ratio of 1.32.
The first subgroup analysis compared studies with the final endpoint during the pandemic with entirely pre-pandemic studies showed that the latter had an odds ratio of 1.35 (95%-CI 1.32-1.51;
Table 2) while the pandemic related studies had an odds ratio of 1.51 (95%-CI: 1.25-1.82).

The second subgroup analysis by endpoint decade showed that the calculated odds ratios for the decades prior to the 2020s were relatively similar, while the pandemic decade of the 2020s had a relatively higher odds ratio (Table 3).

text.text: However, only two included studies were conducted in the 1990s yielding a highly imprecise estimate.
The tests for subgroup differences were nonsignificant (pandemic analysis: p=0.33; end decade analysis: p=0.77).
The third subgroup analysis covered different mental health problems (Table 4).

text.text: This analysis revealed a significant difference between the subgroups (p=0.04), with depression standing out in particular.
Whilst publications reporting a general mental health problem had an odds ratio of 1.29 (95%-CI: 1.14-1.47), those reporting depression had an odds ratio of 1.58 (95%-CI: 1.37-1.83).
To test the robustness of the analyses, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by excluding the samples assessed using DSM instruments (k=7) from the analysis.
This analysis yielded an odds ratio of 1.36 (95% CI: 1.23-1.51).

The meta-regression with moderators world region, mental health problem group, end decade and range of years between first and last data collection yielded no significant model and no significant moderator (Table 5).

text.text: The test for publication bias was not significant (t = -0.43, p = 0.6682), indicating no funnel plot asymmetry (see Funnel Plot, Appendix).
First, as quite often with global epidemiological analyses, the publications used in our data set are based overwhelmingly on samples in the Global North.
Hence, firm conclusions on other world regions cannot be made due to a shortage of studies.
Second, the coverage of mental illhealth problems is unevenly distributed with depression and behavioural problems as the most surveyed conditions in the original studies.

Third, as our analytical approach is focussed on the bigger picture of prevalence change for mental health problems of children and adolescents over time, we cannot rule out that there are temporal fluctuations in terms of prevalence changes between the two time points that we used in our analysis.

This systematic review employed a meta-analysis to examine global prevalence rate changes of mental health problems amongst children and young adolescents based on 58 studies from the period of 1973-2023.
The meta-analysis yielded an odds ratio of 1.38.
The relevant question here is how this effect size should be interpreted.
Is an OR of 1.38 or an OR of 1.51 from studies that had their endpoint during the pandemic a lot or a little?
When interpreting a change in prevalence, it is helpful to first know the baseline, or base rate.

According to a recent meta-analysis of studies conducted between 2015 and 2020, the prevalence of mental disorders among children and adolescents in Europe is approximately 15.5 percent (Sacco et al., 2024).
text.formatted: According to a recent meta-analysis of studies conducted between 2015 and 2020, the prevalence of mental disorders among children and adolescents in Europe is approximately 15.5 percent <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Sacco et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Since our meta-analysis suggests an increase over several decades that date further back, we hypothetically assume a base rate of 12 percent.
At a base rate of 12 percent our estimated odds ratio of 1.38 corresponds to a risk ratio of 1.32.
This means that children and adolescents currently have a 32 percent higher risk of developing a mental disorder compared to previous times.
Translated into prevalence, this would currently be 15.7 percent (a baseline prevalence of 12 percent increased by 32 percent).
Overall, the prevalence of mental problems of children and adolescents would thus have increased by 3.7 percent.
Given the time range of 50 years, we regard this as a minor increase.
When we compare our overall results with those of other meta-studies, we see similar trends and conclusions.

Our assessment that the mental health problems of children and adolescents have only increased slightly, especially in the pre-pandemic phase, is consistent with the metaanalysis of self-report psychosomatic complaints with studies between 1980 and 2013 (Potrebny et al., 2017).

text.text: Our findings can also be interpreted in a similar way to the results of the Global Burden of Disease study (Yang et al., 2024), which reported some fluctuations in prevalence but no increase in prevalence in the age-adjusted analysis.

text.text: Whilst the estimates were numerically higher, the authors cautioned against directly translating these into clinical relevance.
Another meta-analysis of longitudinal studies found standardized differences of 0.1 for anxiety symptoms and 0.26 for depressive symptoms (Madigan et al., 2023).

text.text: Our other findings are also consistent with the general research literature.
We found a significantly greater change in prevalence in studies that reached their endpoint during the pandemic.
This corresponds to the research literature in psychiatric epidemiology for this age group (Samji et al., 2022; Wolf & Schmitz, 2024).
text.formatted: This corresponds to the research literature in psychiatric epidemiology for this age group <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Samji et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Wolf & Schmitz, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, our findings do not support the hypothesis that the 2010s were associated with a particular rise in prevalence, as suggested by Haidt (Haidt, 2024).
text.formatted: However, our findings do not support the hypothesis that the 2010s were associated with a particular rise in prevalence, as suggested by Haidt <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Haidt, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: According to our analysis, the influence of digital tools and social media would be less profound in terms of mental health prevalence changes than is generally assumed.
Furthermore, the higher burden we found among females compared to males is consistent with the research literature (Herrmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the higher burden we found among females compared to males is consistent with the research literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Herrmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although this literature does not report any significant differences between the genders overall, females show a higher burden in the area of internalising disorders, while externalising disorders dominate among males.
However, the primary studies included in our meta-analysis predominantly measured internalising constructs.
Although the pooled estimates suggest an overall small increase, heterogeneity was high, likely reflecting real differences across regions, periods, measures, informants, ages, and conditions.
The pooled effect should be read as an average trend, not a uniform change, and deviations are expected across contexts or between conditions.
However, the meta-regression was unable to identify any significant moderator.

Neither a specific mental health problem, nor a particular region of the world, nor a specific decade, nor the number of years between the first and last data collection proved to be predictive of heterogeneity.
The mental health of children and adolescent is a significant concern with profound implications for service demands in mental health care.
To our knowledge this is the first meta-analysis that calculates pooled prevalence rates of mental health problems from studies in this population which consistently use the most robust design.
The trend we found of only a slight increase in mental health problems does not correspond with the high demand for psychiatric or psychological treatment in this age group.
We therefore conclude that only a small part of the increase in demand is based on changes in the epidemiological prevalence.
Similar to adults, other socio-cultural factors appear to play a role here as well, driving demand for psychiatric services (Richter et al., 2026).
